What makes a woodpecker so amazing?

The woodpecker, the star behind that tapping sound on the trees, is the "forest carpenter" that catches bugs inside the wood with its tough beak.

content.alt: Woodpecker - Nature and science facts about woodpeckers
content.text:
Nature and science facts about woodpeckers

A woodpecker drums on trees with its tough beak (drumming) to find larvae hidden inside. Even when it pecks so fast, its head isn't hurt thanks to a special head structure that absorbs the shock. After making a hole, it pulls out the bugs with its very long, sticky, barbed tongue. It props itself up with stiff tail feathers, and its toes point two forward and two back to grip the tree tightly. The holes a woodpecker digs become homes for other animals, which is why it's called the "forest carpenter."

Parent guide — how to nurture curiosity

Compare its "head structure that stays safe even while hammering fast" to a helmet or a cushion. On a walk, when you hear a woodpecker, saying "it's looking for bugs" makes it even more interesting.

content.text:
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Q. Why doesn't a woodpecker's head get hurt?
A. Even when it pecks so fast, it's thanks to a special head structure that absorbs the shock.

Q. Why is it called the "forest carpenter"?
A. Because the tree holes a woodpecker digs become homes for other birds and animals.

Q. How can we observe woodpeckers at home?
A. Explain the head structure by comparing it to a helmet or cushion, and listen for the tapping sound on a walk.
